rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - three-season field experiment (2018-2019) in a solar greenhouse in Tianjin with four treatments (CIF, CIFS, DIF, DIFS) in three replicates, measuring N2O fluxes (static chambers), N leaching (suction cups at 90 cm) and fruit yield. Q2: Section 3.1 and Fig. 1a - annual tomato yield about 147 t/ha for CIF and in tendency about 10% higher for DIF treatments, straw did not affect yield; Section 3.2/Table 1 - annual N2O 9.6-9.9 kg N/ha for DIF/DIFS vs 47.8-78.5 for CIF/CIFS; Section 3.3/Table 2 - annual NO3 leaching 67-89 kg N/ha in DIF/DIFS vs 603-788 in CIF/CIFS; Discussion opening states drip fertigation with straw cut N2O by 80% and N leaching by 88% while yields stayed stable. Q4: Section 3.4 and Fig. S2 - daily N2O and weekly NO3 leaching correlated with measured soil WFPS, soil temperature and soil mineral N (0-30 cm); Fig. 2c - WFPS more stable under drip; Fig. 5 - plant N uptake 45-48% of input for DIF vs 15-16% for CIF. Q8: Section 4.2 - the study does not answer whether the applied irrigation/fertilisation rates are optimal, which would need modelling and multifactorial experiments the authors could not realise (also Conclusions); Section 4.2 - the strong decline in DON leaching for CIF may be a legacy effect of suction-cup installation creating preferential flow paths. Q9: Fig. 1 (mean <U+00B1> SE, N=9) for yield, WUE, PFPN and N2O; Tables 1 and 2 give seasonal and annual N2O and leaching values with <U+00B1> SE.
rows.notes: Yield is measured by a single method (fresh fruit weight), and N2O and leaching each by one method, so no triangulation. Single site, single crop (tomato), plot scale (6.7 x 3.6 m plots). Q7 set to no with doubt: the authors attribute the strong N-loss reductions to low-amount, high-frequency fertigation and the reduced N rate, and explain differences from Yao et al. (2019) by lower irrigation amount, lower clay content, higher fertigation frequency and lower N rate, but these are offered as explanations rather than stated requirements for the effect. Note that the drip treatment also used a 59% lower N fertiliser rate, so the drip effect is confounded with reduced fertilisation (acknowledged by the authors). Yield difference between DIF and CIF was only 'in tendency' higher, i.e. yields comparable.

notes: Full text appears complete apart from supplementary tables/figures (S1, S2) referenced but not included; Table 1 is garbled by rotation but values are legible.
